title: Mysterious cosmic hum may come from first black hole from over 13 billion ago

content:
A faint “hum” traveling through the universe may contain clues about some of the first giant black holes ever formed. New research from Colgate University suggests that gravitational waves detected today could help scientists investigate events that occurred more than 13 billion years ago, including the possible existence of unusual objects known as dark stars.

The mysterious signal is part of what scientists call the gravitational-wave background. Unlike a single gravitational-wave event, such as the collision of two black holes, this background consists of countless overlapping signals produced throughout the universe.

Scientists detect these extremely low-frequency waves using pulsar timing arrays, which monitor rapidly spinning neutron stars called pulsars.

Pulsars act as some of the most precise clocks in space. They emit regular radio pulses that can be measured from Earth. When gravitational waves travel between a pulsar and Earth, they cause extremely small changes in the timing of those signals.

By studying these changes across numerous pulsars, international research teams have found evidence of a background of gravitational waves.

Scientists generally believe that much of this background comes from pairs of supermassive black holes orbiting one another and gradually moving closer together. However, researchers Sohan Ghodla and Cosmin Ilie wanted to investigate a deeper question: where did the enormous black holes responsible for these signals originally come from?

Their study examined the possibility that some began as remnants of hypothetical objects called dark stars. Despite their name, dark stars are not just ordinary stars without light. Researchers believe these theoretical objects could have formed in the early universe and been powered partly by interactions involving dark matter rather than primarily by nuclear fusion.

Under the conditions considered in the study, dark stars could potentially grow to more than a million times the mass of the Sun before collapsing into massive black holes. Those black holes could then grow alongside their galaxies, eventually merging with other massive black holes billions of years later and producing gravitational waves.

“Pulsar timing arrays are usually thought of as probes of supermassive black-hole binaries in the relatively recent Universe,” Ilie said. “What our work shows is that the signal may also contain information about how the ancestors of those black holes formed at cosmic dawn.”

The researchers modeled how black holes from different early formation pathways could evolve throughout cosmic history. Their results suggested that descendants of supermassive dark stars could potentially contribute a significant, and possibly dominant, portion of the gravitational-wave background measured today.

The findings could also help scientists place limits on how common these early black hole seeds were. “Produce too many of these massive seeds and you end up over-producing the PTA-detected signal,” Ghodla said. “Produce too few, and you need other sources to efficiently assemble these supermassive black holes.”

The study creates a potential connection between dark matter, the universe’s first stars and modern gravitational-wave observations. As pulsar timing array measurements become more precise, scientists may gain a new way to investigate how the universe’s earliest supermassive black holes formed.
